question: A manufacturer of exempt and taxable goods wants to claim a refund of accumulated ITC due to inverted duty structure. Walk through the eligibility conditions, formula, and documentary requirements under Rule 89(5) read with Section 54(3).
ground_truth: Under Section 54(3) of the CGST Act, refund of accumulated ITC is allowed when the rate of tax on inputs is higher than the rate on output supplies (inverted duty structure). Rule 89(5) of CGST Rules prescribes the formula: Maximum Refund = (Turnover of inverted rated supply of goods and services x Net ITC / Adjusted Total Turnover) - Tax payable on such inverted rated supply. Eligibility conditions: (1) Refund only for inverted rated supplies, not exempted supplies. (2) No refund if accumulation is due to ITC on input services. (3) The manufacturer must file refund application in Form GST RFD-01 within 2 years from the end of the financial year. Documentary requirements include: Statement of invoices (Annexure to RFD-01), declaration that ITC has not been availed on excluded supplies, CA certificate/auditor's report for refund above Rs. 2 lakh.

question: A principal manufacturer sends goods to a job worker under a challan. If the goods are not returned within 3 years, what are the ITC consequences? Does the timeline differ for moulds/dies/jigs/fixtures vs. inputs?
ground_truth: Under Section 143 read with Section 19 of the CGST Act: For inputs sent to a job worker, if not returned within 1 year (not 3 years), the principal must pay tax as if the inputs were supplied on the date they were sent. For capital goods (including moulds, dies, jigs, fixtures, and tools) sent to a job worker, the time limit is 3 years. If not returned within 3 years, it is deemed a supply and the principal must pay tax with interest. The timeline explicitly differs: 1 year for inputs, 3 years for capital goods including moulds/dies/jigs/fixtures. The principal can extend these periods by filing an application with the Commissioner.

question: A taxpayer received a demand order under Section 73 that was partially confirmed and partially dropped. Can they settle the confirmed portion under Section 128A amnesty? What is the process on the GST portal (SPL-02)?
ground_truth: Yes, the taxpayer can settle the confirmed portion under Section 128A. The scheme applies to Section 73 demands for FY 2017-18, 2018-19, and 2019-20. For partially confirmed demands, only the confirmed tax portion needs to be paid. Process: (1) Pay the confirmed tax amount via DRC-03. (2) File SPL-01 application referencing the confirmed amount. (3) The proper officer verifies and issues SPL-02 (waiver order) confirming interest and penalty waiver. SPL-02 is not filed by the taxpayer — it is the order issued by the officer after processing SPL-01. If the demand has both Section 73 and Section 74 components, only the Section 73 portion qualifies.

question: A trader (not a manufacturer) wants to claim benefit under the new EMI-based deferred duty payment scheme announced in the 2025 Union Budget. Is a trader eligible? What entity categories qualify?
ground_truth: A trader is NOT eligible for the EMI-based deferred duty payment scheme. The scheme is specifically designed for entities that import goods for use in manufacturing or processing. Eligible categories include: (1) Manufacturers registered under the Factories Act importing raw materials or capital goods for own manufacturing. (2) Authorised Economic Operators (AEO) with T2/T3 certification. (3) Status Holders under Foreign Trade Policy. (4) SEZ/EOU units importing for manufacturing and export. Pure trading entities that buy and resell without value addition do not qualify.

question: A taxpayer wants to file SPL-01 under the Section 128A amnesty but the portal shows an error because their original order was issued under Section 74 and later rectified to Section 73. What is the official workaround per the CBIC circular?
ground_truth: Per CBIC Circular No. 238/32/2024-GST, the taxpayer IS eligible for Section 128A benefit if the order was rectified from Section 74 to Section 73. The official workaround for the portal error is: (1) File the application manually with the jurisdictional proper officer (not through the portal). (2) Attach the rectification order showing the change from Section 74 to Section 73. (3) Alternatively, use FORM GST SPL-05 or SPL-06 and mention the rectification details in the remarks column (Column 19/20). The GSTN portal team has been instructed to enable system-level correction, but until then, manual filing is the accepted route.

question: An importer discovers that they classified goods under the wrong HS code on a past Bill of Entry, resulting in lower duty paid. Can they voluntarily file for reassessment / revision under the new Customs voluntary compliance scheme? What is the process?
ground_truth: Yes, an importer can voluntarily correct a classification error on past Bills of Entry. Under Section 149 of the Customs Act (amendment of documents) and Section 28(5), voluntary disclosure before any investigation attracts no penalty. Process: (1) Calculate the differential duty for each affected Bill of Entry. (2) File a voluntary disclosure with the jurisdictional Commissioner of Customs. (3) Pay the differential customs duty plus interest under Section 28AA (15% per annum). (4) The proper officer issues a reassessment order. (5) Additional IGST paid on import is available as ITC under GST. Benefits: No penalty if disclosed before investigation, reduced interest, and demonstrates good faith.

question: The new GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT) has been operationalized. If a taxpayer in Rajasthan wants to appeal a Rs. 80 lakh demand, which bench has jurisdiction? What is the pre-deposit requirement?
ground_truth: For a taxpayer in Rajasthan, the Jaipur bench of GSTAT has jurisdiction over all appeals from Rajasthan. Pre-deposit requirement: 20% of the disputed tax amount must be deposited (over and above the 10% pre-deposit at the first appellate stage). For an Rs. 80 lakh demand: GSTAT pre-deposit is Rs. 16 lakh (20% of 80 lakh), payable through electronic cash ledger only (not ITC). Since the disputed tax is above Rs. 50 lakh, the appeal will be heard by a Division Bench (1 Judicial + 1 Technical member). Total cumulative pre-deposit at GSTAT stage: Rs. 24 lakh (10% first appeal + 20% GSTAT = 30% of demand).

question: A Tier 4 Urban Co-operative Bank (UCB) wants to offer gold loans to a jewellery manufacturer. What are the RBI restrictions on (a) loan-to-value ratio, (b) end-use monitoring, and (c) aggregate exposure limits specific to a Tier 4 UCB?
ground_truth: (a) LTV ratio: Must not exceed 75% for lending against gold jewellery. Gold jewellery must be valued at the average closing price of 22 carat gold for the preceding 30 days as quoted by IBJA. (b) End-use: Under RBI's amended Lending Against Gold and Silver Collateral Directions (September 2025, RBI/2025-26/84), Tier 3/4 UCBs may extend need-based working capital finance to borrowers using gold as raw material in manufacturing. The borrower must not acquire or hold gold for investment or speculative purposes. Banks cannot grant advances for purchase of gold in any form. (c) Exposure limits: UCBs have aggregate exposure limits — total gold-backed lending should be within the overall single-borrower and group-borrower exposure norms as per the UCB Master Direction.

question: An NBFC registered with RBI is onboarding a new customer. What are the specific UAPA and UN sanctions screening obligations for an NBFC (as distinct from a scheduled commercial bank)? Does the NBFC need to file STRs with FIU-IND?
ground_truth: Per RBI circular RBI/2025-26/94 on UAPA compliance: All Regulated Entities including NBFCs must (1) Ensure no accounts are held for individuals/entities on the UNSC 1267/1989 ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List. (2) Follow the procedure in UAPA Order dated February 2, 2021 (amended April 22, 2024). (3) Forward de-listing requests to Joint Secretary (CTCR), MHA. NBFCs have the same UAPA/UN sanctions screening obligations as scheduled commercial banks — there is no distinction. Yes, NBFCs must file Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) with FIU-IND under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). RBI's KYC Master Direction applies uniformly to all Regulated Entities.

question: An NBFC-Factor registered under the Factoring Regulation Act wants to accept gold inventory as a pledge from a borrower. Is this permitted? What specific RBI directions apply to NBFC-Factors regarding the nature of acceptable collateral?
ground_truth: An NBFC-Factor's primary business is factoring (purchasing receivables), not general lending. Accepting gold inventory as primary collateral for a standalone loan is NOT recommended as it transforms the NBFC into a gold lending entity, violating the principal business criterion (factoring must remain >50% of financial assets). However, gold can be accepted as additional/secondary collateral for a lending transaction. The Factoring Regulation Act Section 5 defines factoring as assignment of receivables — it does not authorize general lending against physical collateral. If the NBFC-Factor does accept gold, it must comply with RBI's gold lending directions: 75% LTV, and the RBI Master Direction on NBFC-ND/SI Directions applies.

question: A GTA (Goods Transport Agency) has a long-term contract at a fixed rate. Mid-contract, the GST rate on GTA services is revised. Who bears the additional GST – the transporter or the recipient? What does the contract's force majeure / change-in-law clause typically need to say?
ground_truth: Under Section 14 of CGST Act, the new rate applies to all supplies made on or after the effective date. The GTA is legally liable to charge the revised rate. Who bears the cost depends on contract terms: if 'inclusive of GST' — the GTA absorbs it; if 'exclusive of GST' or 'plus applicable taxes' — the recipient bears it. A GST rate change is NOT force majeure (it is a foreseeable regulatory action). The contract should have a change-in-law clause with: (1) trigger definition covering indirect tax rate changes, (2) pass-through mechanism on rupee-for-rupee basis, (3) notice requirement within 15 days, (4) adjustment based on date of supply not contract date, (5) renegotiation trigger if rate change exceeds 2 percentage points. If the contract is silent, the GTA must charge the new rate and the recipient may refuse, creating a commercial dispute.

question: A hotel collects an advance for a banquet booking when the GST rate is 18%. Before the event date, the rate is reduced to 12%. Which rate applies – the rate at the time of advance or the rate at the time of supply? Cite the relevant provision and any clarificatory circular.
ground_truth: The 12% rate (new/reduced rate at time of supply) applies. Section 14(b)(ii) of the CGST Act specifically provides that where payment is received before the change in rate but the supply is made after the change, the new rate applies. The hotel must apply 12%, and the excess 6% collected as advance must be refunded or adjusted via credit note. CBIC Circular No. 1/1/2017-GST (Transition) clarified that Section 14 overrides the normal time-of-supply rules in Sections 12/13. The rate at the time of actual supply (event date) determines the applicable rate.

question: An employer procures a group health insurance policy for employees. Is GST charged on the premium eligible for ITC? How does the answer differ if the employer instead reimburses individual employees who buy their own health policy?
ground_truth: Scenario 1 (employer procures group policy): GST on the premium is generally NOT eligible for ITC — blocked under Section 17(5)(b) of CGST Act as health services for employee personal consumption. Exception: ITC is available if the employer is legally obligated to provide health insurance (e.g., under ESI Act or statutory requirement). Scenario 2 (employer reimburses employees): No GST/ITC question arises. The employee purchases in individual capacity, insurer invoices the employee, and the reimbursement is a salary/perquisite — outside the GST framework. The employer receives no GST invoice and cannot claim ITC. Key difference: In Scenario 1, GST cost is borne by employer as non-creditable expense. In Scenario 2, there is no GST invoice to the employer at all.

question: After a GST rate change on a product, does the manufacturer have a legal obligation to reduce the MRP on existing stock? Under which law – GST, Legal Metrology, or Consumer Protection? What has the National Anti-Profiteering Authority / CCI ruled on this?
ground_truth: Under the Legal Metrology Act/Rules, manufacturers are NOT legally required to re-label MRP on existing stock — MRP is a maximum price, and selling below it is permitted. However, under Section 171 of CGST Act (anti-profiteering), any rate reduction must be passed to consumers through commensurate price reduction — this is a GST-specific obligation. The manufacturer must reduce the effective selling price even if the MRP label isn't changed. The NAA (dissolved December 2022, functions transferred to CCI) ruled in multiple cases (HUL, Pyramid Infratech, etc.) that manufacturers must reduce base price to reflect reduced GST on new production, and for existing stock, must sell at effective reduced price. Penalty: Amount of profiteering + 10% penalty. CCI now handles anti-profiteering through the DGAP.

question: If a product's HSN classification is challenged by the department and reclassified to a higher-rate heading, can the department demand differential tax for past years even if the taxpayer relied on a published advance ruling in their favour? What are the limits of an advance ruling's binding effect?
ground_truth: Under Section 103(1) of CGST Act, an advance ruling is binding only on the applicant and the concerned jurisdictional officer for the specific question ruled upon. The department can demand differential tax only after getting the ruling overturned by AAAR or GSTAT — until then, the ruling shields the taxpayer. If the ruling is voided by AAAR, the demand can only be prospective (from the AAAR order date), NOT retrospective, unless fraud/misrepresentation is proved under Section 104. Limits of binding effect: (1) Binding only on the specific applicant, not other taxpayers. (2) State-specific — different AARs may rule differently. (3) Becomes void if obtained by fraud/suppression/misrepresentation (Section 104). (4) Void if law changes. (5) Cannot be obtained for past transactions.

question: A supplier issues a credit note, but the recipient has already accepted the original invoice on the IMS (Invoice Management System). The recipient now wants to reject the credit note. What is the step-by-step process on the GST portal to reverse the ITC adjustment?
ground_truth: Step-by-step process: (1) Navigate to GST Portal → Returns → IMS Dashboard. (2) Filter by document type = 'Credit Note' and search by supplier GSTIN or credit note number. (3) If the credit note shows 'No Action' (pending), select it and click 'Reject'. (4) Confirm rejection — the credit note will NOT reduce ITC in the next GSTR-2B. (5) Supplier is notified of rejection. If the credit note was deemed accepted (auto-accepted after due date), the recipient cannot reverse through IMS — workarounds include: raising a grievance on the portal, asking the supplier to issue a fresh debit note, or manually adding ITC back in GSTR-3B Table 4 with audit trail. Important: Reject before GSTR-2B generation date (typically 14th of the month) for it to reflect in the current period.

question: While filing GSTR-9 (annual return), a taxpayer finds that Table 8A (auto-populated ITC from GSTR-2A/2B) does not match their books. What are the possible reasons for mismatch, and what is the correct way to reconcile and report the difference in Table 8C?
ground_truth: Possible reasons for Table 8A vs books mismatch: (1) Timing differences — invoice in supplier's GSTR-1 in different FY than recipient's claim. (2) Amendments by supplier in subsequent periods. (3) Credit notes issued in different period. (4) GSTR-2A vs GSTR-2B computation differences. (5) Reverse charge ITC not in 8A. (6) Import IGST timing differences. Table 8C reports ITC from current FY invoices claimed in the next FY's returns (before annual return filing date). It is NOT auto-populated — taxpayer must manually calculate and enter. Reconciliation: Download 8A data, compare with ITC register, classify differences into categories (8A has/books don't = report in 8D; books have/8A doesn't = report in 8C or 8F). Net ITC = 8A + 8C - 8D adjustments.

question: A QRMP (Quarterly Return Monthly Payment) taxpayer receives a credit note from a supplier. Under IMS, credit notes are auto-accepted if not acted upon. If the taxpayer disputes the credit note, what happens to the ITC in their next quarterly GSTR-3B?
ground_truth: If the QRMP taxpayer rejects the credit note in IMS during the quarter, the credit note will be excluded from the quarterly GSTR-2B, and ITC will NOT be reduced in the next quarterly GSTR-3B. The ITC remains as claimed from the original invoice. QRMP taxpayers can take IMS actions in any month (M1, M2, M3) of the quarter — all actions are consolidated when quarterly GSTR-2B is generated. If the taxpayer takes no action, the credit note is deemed accepted after the quarterly GSTR-3B filing due date, and ITC WILL be reduced in the next quarter's GSTR-2B. Best practice: Review IMS monthly, reject disputed credit notes immediately upon appearance.

question: RBI has mandated a shift to floating-rate lending for certain loan categories while simultaneously the GST Council has changed the treatment of insurance premiums bundled with loans. For a bank offering a home loan with bundled life insurance, how do these two regulatory changes interact in terms of (a) the EMI structure and (b) the GST invoice to the borrower?
ground_truth: (a) EMI structure: The floating rate reset changes only the interest component. The EMI comprises principal + interest (exempt from GST) + insurance premium (taxable at 18% GST). At each reset, the bank must transparently show the revised breakup. The insurance premium component may be fixed or variable independently of the interest rate. (b) GST invoice: Interest on the loan is exempt from GST. Insurance premium is taxable at 18%. If insurance is optional (not mandatory for loan), each is a separate supply — the insurer or bank (as corporate agent) must issue a separate GST invoice for the insurance premium. If insurance is mandatory (composite supply), the principal supply is the exempt loan, potentially making the whole supply exempt — though IRDAI and RBI discourage mandatory bundling. The borrower generally cannot claim ITC on insurance (personal use for residential; blocked under Section 17(5) for commercial).

question: A manufacturer in a state that offers a capital investment subsidy (treated as exempt from GST) finds that a GST rate increase on their output product effectively nullifies the subsidy benefit. Can they challenge the rate change as violating the state incentive scheme? What legal remedies exist at the GST Council and High Court level?
ground_truth: Challenging the rate change directly is very difficult — courts hold there is no vested right to a particular tax rate, and the GST Council has sovereign power to recommend rate changes. Promissory estoppel does not apply against legislative/sovereign power (Supreme Court in Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills). Available remedies: (1) GST Council representation — through the state Finance Minister who is a Council member, request rate review or special provision for subsidy beneficiaries. (2) Approach state government to increase the subsidy to compensate for the higher rate (since subsidies must go through the budgetary route per GST Council's 3rd/5th meeting decisions). (3) Writ petition under Article 226 in High Court — argue promissory estoppel against the state (not the rate change), Article 14 arbitrariness if rate change disproportionately affects subsidized industries. (4) Contractual/arbitration route if the subsidy agreement has a change-in-law clause. The practical recommendation is to exhaust representation and negotiation before litigation.
